text:
Self-reflection is a good place to start, but it can’t see what it can’t see.

A peer can give another angle. Your partner is also usually trying to keep you, so they have an ulterior motive that a peer counselor hopefully does not.

I recommend peer counseling outside the couple: if my partner is the only person I bring all my pain to, she also ends up carrying whatever I do when I still don’t understand it.

I also have to deal with what happens in my body: my mind may understand that my partner is going through something difficult and that I don’t have to be dragged down with her, but my body still feels dragged down, fragile, and sensitive. My breathing gets shallow, and it becomes extremely hard to feel okay while she is in pain.

Crying helps a lot, but it may actually be harder for men once they are in a relationship because they are expected to be the shoulder everybody else cries on. That is another reason to have a peer counselor.

Crying also contains a type of automatic erratic breathwork. Breathwork is one of the easiest ways I know to calm down. Reduced breathing or the Buteyko method is especially useful to me when my partner is getting me upset and flustered with drama. Sometimes she’s deliberately trying to do that, and other times it’s hard to tell. I explain more of the body-based options in my Somatic Modalities guide.

Meditation is also helpful, but for most people, I would still put inner-child reparenting, peer counseling, and body-based work first or make them primary meditation targets. Many people say they cannot meditate or have not gotten to that stage yet, and meditation without grounding in those approaches can easily be a road into spiritual bypassing.

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
